title: Theorem
body_md: Let \((\Lambda,\mathcal{T}^*)\) be an LVMB configuration with \(k\) indispensable indices. Let \(N = N(\Lambda,\mathcal{T}^*)\) be the corresponding LVMB manifold, then \(\dim_{\mathrm{alg}}\!\left(N\right) \leq a(\Lambda) + \max\left(0,\left\lfloor \frac{k-1}{2} \right\rfloor\right)\). In particular, for any LVMB manifold with \(k \leq 2\), we have \(\dim_{\mathrm{alg}}\!\left(N\right) = a(\Lambda)\).

body_md: The definition of triangulated vector configuration allows some vectors in \(V\) not to belong to any simplex of \(\mathcal{T}\). These will be called \emph{ghost vectors}, and up to a permutation of the indices, they can be put at the head of \(V\) as \(v_1, \dots, v_k\).

label: adding_no_more_than_2_ghosts
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{adding_no_more_than_2_ghosts}
    Any triangulated vector configuration \((V,\mathcal{T})\) can be turned into an odd and balanced one by adding no more than two ghost vectors. Balancedness can be achieved by prepending \(-\sum_i v_i\) to \(V\) and increasing \(n\) by 1; oddness, in turn, can be obtained just by prepending one or two copies of \(0\) to \(V\) and correspondingly increasing \(n\).

label: indispensableRemark
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{indispensableRemark}
    Gale duality is what connects triangulated vector configurations to LVMB data. In particular, as the indices of ghost vectors belong to any \(\tau^* \in \mathcal{T}^*\), the corresponding coordinates in \(U(\mathcal{T})\) never vanish. In the literature, these are known as \emph{indispensable indexes} \cite{Meersseman2000}. From this perspective, the Gale Transform makes ghost vectors correspond to indispensable points of the LVMB datum.

label: Meersseman_lower_bound
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Meersseman_lower_bound}
    Let \(N=N(\Lambda,\mathcal{T}^*)\) be an LVMB manifold with \(k\) indispensable indices, then \(\dim_{\mathrm{alg}}\!\left(N\right) \geq a(\Lambda)\). Moreover, if \(k=0\), then \(\dim_{\mathrm{alg}}\!\left(N\right) = a(\Lambda)\).

title: Note
body_md: More precisely, this theorem is proved only for LVM manifolds---a large subclass of LVMB manifolds (see \cite[\S 4]{BattagliaZaffran2015}). Nevertheless, the proof in \cite{Meersseman2000} extends in every part to the more general LVMB setting, hence we treat this as already proven in the form of the statement above.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Any LVMB manifold arising from a configuration \((\Lambda,\mathcal{T}^*)\) in which all the indices are indispensable is a complex torus \cite{Meersseman2000} (see also the examples in \cite{Thiella2026preprint}). Since in this case \(d = 0\), we have \(a(\Lambda) = 0\). On the other hand, any complex torus---abelian varieties included---can be constructed as an LVMB manifold \cite{Meersseman2000}; thus there is at least one case of an LVMB manifold \(N\) where \(0 = a(\Lambda) < \dim_{\mathrm{alg}}\!\left(N\right)\).
    The fact that the algebraic dimension of a complex torus depends on the \emph{quadratic} relations among the coefficients of its period matrix \cite[\S 2.6]{BirkenhakeLange1999} shows that the algebraic dimension of an LVMB manifold cannot depend solely on the linear information encoded in \((\Lambda,\mathcal{T}^*)\). Indeed, it is classically known that the algebraic dimension of a complex torus of dimension \(k\) may attain any value between \(0\) and \(k\).

title: Note
body_md: From now on, we adopt the following convention: given an equivalence class of configurations \([\Lambda]_{\mathbb{C}}\) of \(n\) points in the affine space \(\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{C}}^m\), we can always choose a representative \(\Lambda\) such that \(\Lambda_1 = 0\). Hence, we can identify such a configuration with the list of vectors \((\Lambda_2,\dots, \Lambda_n)\) in \({\mathbb{C}}^m\). Correspondingly, we will always  identify \(\operatorname{Rel}_\text{aff}(\Lambda) \cong \operatorname{Rel}(\Lambda_2, \dots, \Lambda_n)\) with a subspace of \({\mathbb{R}}^{n-1}\), and similarly identify \(I(\Lambda)\) as a subgroup of \({\mathbb{Z}}^{n-1}\).

label: compact_intersection
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{compact_intersection}
    Let \((\Lambda,\mathcal{T})\) be an LVMB datum with \(k \geq 1\), and let \(0,\Lambda_2,\dots,\Lambda_{k}\) be its indispensable points. We denote as \({\mathbb{R}}^{n-k}_{\geq 0}\) the closure of the positive orthant in \({\mathbb{R}}^{n-k}\). Then, for any \(J \in {\mathbb{R}}^{k-1} \times {\mathbb{R}}^{n-k}_{\geq 0}\), the subset \((J + \operatorname{Rel}(\Lambda)) \cap ({\mathbb{R}}^{k-1} \times {\mathbb{R}}^{n-k}_{\geq 0})\) is compact.

title: Remark
body_md:
In general, \(\mathcal{M}_{X}(X)/{\mathbb{C}}\) fails to be purely transcendental; that is, for no transcendence basis \(\{\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_a\}\) is the extension \(\mathcal{M}_{X}(X)/{\mathbb{C}}(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_a)\) trivial. Indeed, in general this extension is simple and algebraic \cite[Ch.~10, \S6.5]{GrauertRemmert1984}, meaning that it is generated by some element \(\theta \in \mathcal{M}_{X}(X)\) that is algebraic over \({\mathbb{C}}(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_a)\). If \(\theta \in {\mathbb{C}}(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_a)\), then \(\Phi_X^0\) can be taken as \(\Phi_X^0 : X \mathrel{
    \tikz[baseline]{\draw[dash pattern=on .25em off .1 em,->](0,.58ex)--(1 em,.58ex)}} \mathbb{C}\mathrm{P}^a\). Since this map is dominant, such a manifold \(X\) must be rational. The converse holds as well: if \(X\) is rational then \(\mathcal{M}_{X}(X) \cong {\mathbb{C}}(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_a)\).
